schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A AS X, B AS Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A AS X, A AS Y, B AS Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.YA = Z.YB UNION ALL SELECT 1 AS AX FROM A AS X WHERE 1 = 0
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A AS X, B AS Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A AS X, A AS Y, B AS Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.YA = Z.YB UNION ALL SELECT 1 AS AX FROM A AS X WHERE 1 = 0
counterexample: INSERT INTO A (X, YA) VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20); INSERT INTO B (YB) VALUES (10);
explanation: Q1 retrieves distinct values of X from table A where the YA column in A matches the YB column in B. Q2, on the other hand, attempts to join A with itself and B on specific conditions, and then uses UNION ALL to combine the results with a constant value 1, which is never actually used due to the WHERE clause condition 1 = 0 that makes the entire UNION ALL part of the query ineffective.
counterexample_dsp: The difference between Q1 and Q2 is evident when the join conditions are not met, leading Q1 to return no results, while Q2, due to the ineffective UNION ALL, also returns no results. However, if the join conditions are met, Q1 will return the distinct values of X, whereas Q2 will still return no results due to the ineffective UNION ALL.
